How can contractors find jobs from newly issued building permits?

By PermitsByCounty Research Team · Published October 18, 2026 · Guides & Answers

QUICK ANSWER

Yes — newly issued building permits are public records, and they are one of the earliest signals that work is about to start. A permit is usually filed days or weeks before a crew breaks ground, and it names the project, the type of work, the value, and the company that pulled it. Contractors who check new permits every week see jobs before they are posted anywhere else — and the raw data is free from the city or county that issued it.

The short version

  • Permits are public and early. Anyone can read them, and they show up days or weeks before work starts.
  • Each permit tells you four things: the job, the trade it needs, the project value, and the company to call.
  • The free method takes about 30 minutes a week. No paid lead service is required to start.
  • Speed matters. The first subcontractor to call is usually the one who makes the short list.

Why do building permits point to real jobs?

A permit is not a rumor, and it is not a “maybe” project. Before a city or county issues a building permit, somebody has already paid a fee, filed plans, and waited for an approval. People do not pay permit fees for jobs they might do someday. An issued permit means the project is real, funded, and cleared to start.

The second reason is timing. Permits are filed before the work begins — while the builder is still lining up crews, ordering materials, and setting the schedule. That gap is your window. By the time a job shows up on a bid board or a lead site, the general contractor often already has two or three names in mind. A fresh permit puts you in front of the builder before that list is written.

2–6 weeks

Permits are typically filed 2 to 6 weeks before ground breaks on a project — which is why permit data is used to spot jobs early.

Source: Shovels, building-materials supplier guide · Checked October 18, 2026

Think of it this way: a permit is tomorrow’s work, posted in public today. The only question is whether you look at it this week, or hear about the job after another crew is already on site.

What does one permit actually tell you?

A permit record looks dry at first. It is just a row of fields. But each field answers a question you would otherwise have to guess at:

  • Issued date — the day the permit was approved. This tells you how fresh the job is. Fresh is everything: a permit from this week is a project about to start.
  • Permit type — the kind of work: a new home, a roof, a solar install, a remodel, an electrical upgrade. This tells you whether the job needs your trade.
  • Project value — the dollar value written on the application. A $400,000 new home and a $6,000 water-heater swap are both “permits,” but they are not the same phone call. Value tells you the size of the job.
  • Status — “issued” means approved and ready to build. Permits still “in review” may change or stall, so issued permits are the ones to work first.
  • Who pulled it — the general contractor, builder, or company named on the permit. This is the name that matters. That company hires the trades.
  • Location — the project address or area, so you can judge the drive and stay inside the zone you actually serve.

One rule matters here: use the business facts on the permit — the company, the project, the trade. Never go after a homeowner’s personal contact details. The work flows through the builder or contractor on the record, and that is who you call.

The free method, step by step

Here is the whole method. It costs nothing but a little time each week, and it works in any county that posts its permits online.

Step 1: Pick your county and find its permit search. Most mid-size and large cities and counties publish issued permits on an open-data site or a permit search page, free to anyone. Three examples: the City of Austin posts every issued construction permit in a public dataset (Austin Issued Construction Permits), the City of Houston runs a permit search, and Miami-Dade County offers a permit search as well. Search your county’s name plus “issued permits” or “open data” and you will usually find yours.

5.6 million+ views

The City of Austin’s free Issued Construction Permits dataset alone has been viewed more than 5.6 million times — proof of how many builders, suppliers, and contractors already mine this public data.

Source: City of Austin open data portal · Checked October 18, 2026

Step 2: Filter by issued date and your trade. Set the issued date to the last 7 days. Then filter the permit type to your trade — roofing, plumbing, HVAC, electrical, solar, concrete, whatever you do. A short, fresh list beats a huge stale one every time.

Step 3: Sort by project value, high to low. Big value usually means a bigger job and a builder with a real budget. Work the top of the list first. Small jobs are fine filler work, but they should not eat the time you set aside for this.

Step 4: Write down who pulled each permit. For every permit in your trade, note the general contractor or builder named on it, the project, and the value. Names repeat fast in a local market — after a few weeks you will know exactly who is building in your county.

Step 5: Reach out fast, and keep it short and specific. Call or email the company within days, while the job is still being staffed. Name the project, name your trade, and say when you can start. A simple script that works:

“Hi, this is [your name] with [your company]. I saw the permit come through this week for the [new home / remodel / roof] over on [street or neighborhood]. We do [your trade] work here in [county], we are licensed and insured, and we have room in our schedule starting [date]. Would it help if I sent over a price for the [trade] part of that job?”

That is it. No pitch deck, no pressure. You are not begging for work — you are saving the builder a search.

Step 6: Repeat every week, and track the repeat builders. One week of permits is a list. Ten weeks of permits is a map of your market. Keep a simple note of every builder who pulls permits again and again — those are steady customers hiding in plain sight, and a short check-in call every month or two keeps you first in line when their current sub falls through.

How much work is actually out there?

Short answer: a lot, and it never stops. Permits are filed every working day, in every busy county, whether the economy is hot or slow — roofs still leak, families still remodel, and builders still build.

4,836 permits · about $1.8 billion

New residential permits reported across Texas in a single month (September 2026), with Dallas leading at 1,968 permits and Houston close behind.

Source: HBWeekly, Texas residential construction reporting · Checked October 18, 2026

That is one state and one month, for homes alone. The flow of new permitted work is constant. The only real question is who sees it first — the contractor who checks the new permits every week, or the one who waits for the phone to ring.

What do others charge for building permit leads?

Plenty of companies sell this exact same public data, gathered and sorted for you. For example, PermitLeads charges $297–$497 a month for permit leads in Travis County, Texas (pool, fence, deck, and roof permits), according to its pricing page. There is nothing dishonest about that — you are paying for convenience, not for secret data. The records underneath are the same free public records described above.

So the honest trade-off is simple. Do it yourself and it costs about 30 minutes a week. Pay a service and you save the 30 minutes. Either way, the method in this guide is the engine — and if you want a fuller plain-English walkthrough of why permit records work as leads, this dev.to explainer on permits as construction leads makes the same case from a builder’s point of view.

Mistakes that waste your time

  • Chasing old permits. A permit issued 60 or more days ago usually means the crews are already picked and working. Spend your calls on this week’s list.
  • Calling outside your trade or your area. A commercial permit two counties away is not a lead, it is a distraction. Filter hard: your trade, your ground, your size of job.
  • Going after homeowner personal information. Do not. It is not needed, it is not right, and it can get you in trouble. Work through the general contractor or company named on the permit — they are the ones hiring.
  • Giving up after one week. The first week builds the list. The money shows up when a builder sees your name every week and calls you the day his regular sub is booked out. Quitting early is the most common mistake of all.

A simple 30-minute weekly routine

You do not need a system. You need a habit. Here is the routine, one small block at a time:

  • Monday — pull the list (10 minutes). Open your county’s permit search, filter to the last 7 days and your trade, sort by value.
  • Tuesday — shortlist (5 minutes). Pick the permits worth a call: right trade, right area, real value. Note the builder on each one.
  • Wednesday — make the calls (10 minutes). Use the short script from Step 5. Specific and fast beats long and fancy.
  • Friday — follow up (5 minutes). Call back the no-answers once. Short and polite. Then you are done for the week.

Frequently asked questions

Is it legal to use permit data to find work?

Yes. Building permits are public records, and anyone can read them. Use the business contact details of the company on the permit, follow do-not-call rules, and never collect or use a homeowner’s personal information.

How fast should I call after a permit is issued?

Within a few days. Permits are usually filed 2 to 6 weeks before ground breaks, so a fresh permit means the builder is lining up trades right now. A permit that is 60 days old usually means the crew is already picked.

Do I need to pay for permit leads?

No. The raw permit data is free from the city or county that issued it. Paid services charge for convenience — they gather and sort the same public records for you. If your time is worth more than about 30 minutes a week, paying can make sense; the data itself is never the paid part.

Which permits should my trade watch?

Watch permits in your own trade type first — roofing permits if you roof, solar permits if you install solar. Then watch new-construction and remodel permits with real project value, because those jobs need almost every trade.

What if my county has no online permit search?

Call the county or city permit office and ask for the issued-permits list. Many offices post a weekly file or will email one. Ask for permits issued in the last 7 days, with the permit type, project value, and the company that pulled each one.

Sources

  • Shovels — permits filed 2–6 weeks before ground breaks: shovels.ai/building-materials
  • City of Austin — Issued Construction Permits dataset (viewed 5.6 million+ times): data.austintexas.gov
  • City of Houston — permit search: permits.houstontx.gov
  • Miami-Dade County — permit search: miamidade.gov
  • HBWeekly — Texas new residential permits, September 2026 (4,836 permits, about $1.8B; Dallas 1,968): blog.hbweekly.com
  • PermitLeads — Travis County permit lead pricing ($297–$497/month): permitleads.app
  • Explainer — “Building permits are the best construction leads nobody uses”: dev.to

How can I look up building permits by address for free?

By PermitsByCounty Research Team · Published October 18, 2026 · Guides & Answers

QUICK ANSWER

Yes — in most places it is free. Building permits are public records, and most cities and counties let you search them online by address at no cost. You type the address into the permit search for the city or county that issued the permits, and you can see what work was permitted, when, and whether the permit was closed. Where PermitsByCounty covers a county, we gather those records into one place so you do not have to fight the government portal.

The short version

  • Permits are public records, and the lookup is usually free. Most cities and counties let anyone search them online by address.
  • The trick is searching the right office. The city issues permits inside city limits; the county issues them outside. Search the wrong office and you find nothing.
  • Each result shows the basics: the type of work, the date, the status, the reported value, and the company that pulled the permit.
  • Buying a house? Check before you close. An open permit — or big work with no permit at all — is a red flag worth settling first.

First — who issued the permit? (the step everyone gets wrong)

There is no single national permit database. Every permit is issued by one local office, and that office is the only one holding the record. Inside city limits, the city’s building department issues the permits. Outside city limits — in an unincorporated area, which simply means land that is not part of any city — the county issues them.

This is where most lookups go wrong. You search the county site for a house that sits inside a city, the search comes back empty, and it looks like the house has no permit history at all. The records exist — you were asking the wrong office.

Three examples make it plain. Austin’s permits live in a City of Austin dataset. Chicago’s permits live in the City of Chicago’s data portal. But a house in an unincorporated part of Cook County is not in Chicago’s system — it is in Cook County’s own records. Same metro area, different record books.

The fast way to tell: if the address is inside a city, start with the city. If the city search finds nothing, try the county before you decide the work was never permitted.

Step by step: the free building permit lookup by address

Step 1: Write down the exact address. Get the full street address, the unit number if there is one, and the ZIP code. Permit systems are picky — “104 Main St” and “104 Main Street, Apt 4” can return different results.

Step 2: Find the right search. Here are four real ones, all free: the City of Austin’s Issued Construction Permits dataset, the Chicago Data Portal building permits, the City of Houston’s permit search, and Miami-Dade County’s permit search. If your city or county is not on that list, search the web for your city or county name plus “permit search” — most offices have one.

Step 3: Search by the address. Start with the full address. If nothing shows, widen the search a little at a time: drop the unit number, then the ZIP code, then search the street name alone and scan down the list. Small typing differences hide real records.

Step 4: Open each permit and read it. A list of permit numbers does not tell you much by itself. Open each one — the next section explains every field in plain words.

Step 5: Save what you find. Print the results or save a copy. If you are buying the house, hand the list to your agent or your home inspector. It gives them the exact questions to ask the seller.

How to read what you find

A permit record is a short row of fields. Here is what each one means:

  • Permit number — the office’s ID number for that one permit. If you ever call the office, this is the number to give them.
  • Type — the kind of work: a roof, a remodel, electrical, plumbing, new construction, and so on.
  • Issue date — the day the office approved the permit.
  • Status — where the permit stands. “Issued” means approved, and the work may start. “Finaled” or “closed” means the work passed its final inspection and the file is complete — the clean ending you want to see. “Open” means the work was approved but never got that final sign-off. “Expired” means the permit ran out of time before it was closed.
  • Reported value — the project cost written on the application. It is the applicant’s estimate, not an official valuation of the house.
  • Who pulled it — the contractor or company named on the permit. That is a business fact from the public record.

One boundary worth knowing: a permit is a record about work on a property. It tells you what was built, changed, or fixed — it is not a file on the people who live there.

Buying a house? The two checks that matter

If you are buying, do this lookup before you close, not after. Two things matter most, and both are easy to miss.

Check 1: open permits. An open permit means work was approved and started but never passed its final inspection, so the file was never closed. After you buy, that open file can become your problem: closing it may take inspections, fees, or fixing work you did not do. In Florida, open permits are known for surfacing in the days right before closing, and they can hold up a sale until they are sorted out. Finding them early — while the seller can still deal with them — is the whole point of checking.

Check 2: big work with no permit at all. A new addition, a converted garage, a finished basement — with no permit record behind it — may be unpermitted work, meaning no inspector ever looked at it. That does not prove the work is bad, and this post cannot tell you what it means for your sale. Ask the seller about it directly, and talk it through with your agent or your inspector before you close.

One honest note: we are not lawyers, and permit rules differ from city to city. For anything that could affect a purchase, check with your agent, your inspector, or another local professional who knows your area.

If your search finds nothing

An empty result has four common causes. Work through them before you conclude anything:

  • Wrong office. You searched the city for a county property, or the county for a city property. Try the other office.
  • Older paper records. Many offices keep older permits on paper or in scanned files that never made it into the online search.
  • Address format. The office may record the address slightly differently from how you typed it. Try the variations from Step 3.
  • The work was never permitted. Also possible, especially on older houses and do-it-yourself projects.

The next step is simple: call the permit office and ask. Staff search these records all day, and a records request is free or cheap in most places. Ask for the full permit history for the address, and ask how far back their records go.

Frequently asked questions

Is it really free to look up building permits by address?

Yes, in most places. City and county permit searches online are free to use, and the records themselves are public. The only cost that ever shows up is a small copy fee when an office has to pull and copy an old paper file for you.

Can I see permits for a house I don’t own?

Yes. Building permits are public records, so anyone can look them up — buyers, neighbors, contractors, anyone. You do not need the owner’s permission, and you do not need a reason.

How far back do permit records go?

It varies by office. Big cities often have 10 to 30 or more years of permits searchable online. Older records usually still exist, but they sit in the office’s paper or scanned files — you request those from the permit office directly.

What does an open permit mean for a house sale?

An open permit means work was approved and started but never passed its final inspection, so the file was never closed. It can delay a closing until it is resolved, and after the sale it can become the buyer’s problem. Ask your agent how it is handled in your area before you close.

Will the owner be notified that I looked up their permits?

No. Permit records are public, and searching them is not reported to the property owner. Offices do not send notices when someone views a public permit record online.
